statement: 1. One public model name can sit in front of several copies of the model; the chapter calls the copies deployments. [FAILURE-034]
story_cause: Behind one model name, the router can hold several copies of the model, called deployments
note: Terms block: deployment is one litellm_params entry with a model id; model group is the public model_name several deployments share (FAILURE-034).

statement: 2. When a call to one copy fails, the router decides whether to bench that copy: a short timed pause, called a cooldown, so new requests go to the other copies. [FAILURE-021, RDISP-191]
story_cause: The router may bench that deployment for a few seconds, a pause called a cooldown, so new requests go to its other deployments
note: FAILURE-021 returns True only when an entry was written; selection removes cooled ids (RSELECT-044).

statement: 3. Before any rule applies, nine checks can veto the bench, for example an unknown deployment, a failure of the caller's own key, a zero cooldown time, or a provider-default deployment. [FAILURE-022]-[FAILURE-030]
story_cause: They stop it for an unknown deployment, a failure of the caller's own credential, a request rejected before the call, or a personal Copilot session or credential
note: Gates 1, 2, 6 and 9 of FAILURE-022 to FAILURE-030 are exactly these four. The status gate (8) can be overridden by a deployment-level per-type policy (FAILURE-032), and a lone 402 is stopped separately (FAILURE-035); neither makes the statement false.

statement: 4. Under default settings a 401 or 404 benches the copy at once, even when it is the only copy. [FAILURE-044]
story_cause: Under default settings, when no check stops it, one 401 or 404 benches a deployment at once, even a lone one
note: FAILURE-044: should_retry is false for 401 and 404, so the last rate-based rule cools down even a single-deployment group.

statement: 5. A 429 benches the copy unless it is the only one. [FAILURE-043]
story_cause: One 429 benches it unless it is lone
note: FAILURE-043 rule 1: 429 and not single-deployment gives cooldown. A lone 429 falls through to the 1000-request rule and then to no cooldown (should_retry(429) is true).

statement: 6. A 500 does not bench on its own: it needs over half of at least 5 recent requests, counted on that one server, to have failed. [FAILURE-043, FAILURE-073]
story_cause: One 500 does not: a 5xx benches only when over half of at least 5 requests in this server's 60-second window failed, or all of 1000 for a lone one
note: True for a copy that is not lone (FAILURE-043 rule 3, FAILURE-045 per-process counts, FAILURE-073 fixed 60 s window). The statement leaves out 'not lone'; statement 13 carries the lone case, so the two together are consistent.

statement: 7. A bench lasts 5 seconds unless something sets it otherwise. [FAILURE-048, RDISP-191]
story_cause: the deployment's own setting, else the error's retry-after header, else the router's, 5 seconds by default
note: RDISP-191: deployment cooldown_time >= 0, else retry-after >= 0, else router cooldown_time defaulting to 5 s.

statement: 8. The bench is one entry in a shared store (Redis), and other servers usually notice it within about a second. [FAILURE-052, FAILURE-009]
story_cause: When the servers share a store, the others usually see the pause within about a second
note: The reader dropped the condition. The entry sits in the router's own memory tier and is also in Redis only when the router has Redis (FAILURE-001, FAILURE-006, FAILURE-187); without Redis no other server sees it, and with Redis the one-second figure is the read interval (FAILURE-009). Stated flat, a reader cannot tell whether their deployment shares benches.

statement: 9. A bench shorter than one second stays on one server, so the other servers keep sending traffic to that copy. [FAILURE-006]
story_cause: A pause shorter than one second stays on one server, so the others keep sending it traffic
note: FAILURE-006: EX 0 write to Redis is rejected and swallowed (FAILURE-203); entry stays in this process's memory.

statement: 10. After that the router may retry the same group, then try backup models from a list, skipping any it already tried. [FAILURE-103, FAILURE-145]
story_cause: The router may then retry, and after that try backup models from a list, skipping any entry it already tried
note: Retry loop first, then the fallback dispatcher (RDISP-096); attempted set skip in FAILURE-145.

statement: 11. If every copy is benched and no backup model answers, the caller gets a 429 "try again" error. [FAILURE-179, RDISP-115]
story_cause: If every deployment is paused and no backup model answers, the caller gets a "try again" error
note: FAILURE-179: status 429, message 'No deployments available for selected model, Try again in N seconds'; RDISP-115 raises the original exception when no fallback succeeds.

statement: 12. Prometheus numbers can record benches, but the bench itself alerts nobody. [FAILURE-056]
story_cause: the bench itself alerts no one
note: FAILURE-052 and FAILURE-056: the only thing the bench triggers is the two Prometheus calls, and only when a Prometheus logger is registered. The Slack alert is a separate path for a failed call (FAILURE-175 to FAILURE-177).

statement: 13. A lone copy that returns 429s or 500s mostly keeps getting traffic, because it needs 1000 requests in a minute failing before it is benched. [FAILURE-043]
story_cause: Under default settings, a 429 or 5xx never benches a lone deployment unless all of at least 1000 requests in a minute failed, so the router keeps sending to it
note: FAILURE-043/044. True at default settings; a router-level allowed_fails other than 3 or an allowed_fails_policy would bench a lone copy after the count passes (FAILURE-046). The statement omits 'all' and 'default settings' but is not misleading.

statement: 14. The first 50 characters of the error text are stored unmasked, so a key echoed early in an error could leak into the shared store and logs. [FAILURE-210]
story_cause: A stored cooldown keeps the first 50 characters of the error text unmasked, so a key echoed early in a provider error can reach the shared store and the logs
note: FAILURE-003, FAILURE-204, FAILURE-210 (Redis, debug-info cooldown list, INFO log).

statement: 15. The "try again in" number in the 429 may not be the real time left. [FAILURE-017, FAILURE-178]
story_cause: The "try again in" number is the shortest configured cooldown, not the time left on any cooldown
note: FAILURE-017 and FAILURE-178: value is the smallest stored cooldown_time among the model's deployments, not remaining time.

statement: If one copy of a model starts failing or hitting rate limits, the router can set that copy aside for a few seconds, 5 by default, and send requests to your other copies, then try the backup models you list.
story_cause: The router may bench that deployment for a few seconds, a pause called a cooldown, so new requests go to its other deployments
note: Hedged with 'can'. Benching depends on status and failure rate (FAILURE-031, FAILURE-043), so not every failure sets the copy aside, but the sentence does not say it does.

statement: If every copy is set aside and no backup answers, your callers get a 429 "try again" error.
story_cause: If every deployment is paused and no backup model answers, the caller gets a "try again" error

statement: I would check one thing first: if you have only a single copy of a model, the router will keep sending it traffic through most errors, so I would ask an engineer how your setup behaves before promising automatic failover.
story_cause: Under default settings, a 429 or 5xx never benches a lone deployment unless all of at least 1000 requests in a minute failed, so the router keeps sending to it
note: The fact is true at default settings (FAILURE-043/044; a lone 401 or 404 still benches). The advice is too unspecific to act on and blends two things: a bench decides which copy gets new requests, while retries and backup models run after a failed call whether or not anything was benched (FAILURE-103, FAILURE-114, FAILURE-145). The claims do not make backup-model fallback depend on the bench, and a router-level allowed_fails or allowed_fails_policy changes the lone-copy answer (FAILURE-046), which is the question to ask the engineer.

lost: lone deployment: the only deployment of its model group, when the router has no other deployment it may use instead for that request
fix: Say what the extra clause covers: 'only one copy under this model name, or its siblings cannot take this request, for example a sibling reserved for another team or sitting in the same routing group'. Give one example, since FAILURE-034 counts routing-group members and non-blocked team siblings as alternatives.

lost: Nine ordered checks can stop a bench before any rule decides
fix: Replace the single sentence with a numbered list of the nine checks in order: unknown deployment; caller's own credential failed; request rejected before the call; per-user Copilot session on the request; per-user Copilot credential on the deployment; zero cooldown time; cooldowns turned off; status that needs no bench; provider-default deployment. Nine items, nine names.

lost: a personal Copilot session or credential
fix: Say that GitHub Copilot is one of the providers the router can call, and that each user brings their own login for it, so one user's failure says nothing about the shared copy and is never benched.

lost: a request rejected before the call
fix: Say 'a request the router refused as malformed before it reached any provider, so the copy did nothing wrong' (FAILURE-024).

lost: a failure of the caller's own credential ... such as a stored key that was rejected or rate-limited
fix: Say 'a key that the caller saved with the router and that the provider rejected or throttled; that is one caller's problem, so the copy shared by everyone is left in service' and drop 'stored' if it is not needed.

lost: provider-default deployment: a deployment the router lists as a provider's default
fix: Say 'copies the router set up on its own as a provider's default entry, as opposed to ones the operator configured; the router keeps a list of these ids and never benches them', and say who fills the list (the router's configuration, FAILURE-030).

lost: a status that needs no bench
fix: Give the rule in plain words once: 'every 4xx except 429, 401, 402, 404 and 408 needs no bench; 2xx, 3xx and 5xx statuses go on to the next step; an empty status or an error whose text contains APIConnectionError needs no bench' (FAILURE-031).

lost: Before the three rules, a 402 on a lone deployment ends with no cooldown
fix: Name the three rules where they are first used (deployment allowance, failure-rate rules, router counter) and refer to them by those names in the steps; write 'before any of the three rules' and keep the 'counts the failure, picks a cooldown time and asks for a decision' sentence clearly separate from them.

lost: The deployment's own numbers come first: A deployment with its own allowance gets counted with its number for this error, or with the router's number when it has none for this error
fix: Rewrite as a lookup order: 'use the deployment's number for this kind of error; if it has none for this error, the deployment's plain number; if it has neither, the router's number.' Say which number applies when (FAILURE-040, FAILURE-047).

lost: "allowance" vs "allowed-fails policy" vs "allowed-fails counter" vs "retry policy" vs "retry count": five similar terms
fix: Define each by what it does, not what it is not: allowance = number of failures forgiven before a bench; allowed-fails policy = a different allowance per kind of error; allowed-fails counter = the running tally of failures compared with the allowance; retry count = how many times a failed request is sent again to the same model name; retry policy = a different retry count per kind of error. Show them once side by side.

lost: an allowance of 1 benches on the second failure, and 0 on the first
fix: Say 'the allowance is how many failures are forgiven: with 0 forgiven the first failure benches; with 1 forgiven the second failure benches'.

lost: The router compares its own failure allowance with the library-wide default, 3 unless changed; an equal value counts as unset
fix: Say 'the software ships with a built-in allowance of 3; if the operator sets the router's allowance to exactly 3, the router acts as if nothing was set and uses the failure-rate rules instead of the counter'. Mark it as a known quirk likely unintended (FAILURE-208), so customers who set 3 on purpose know to expect the rate rules.

lost: A lone deployment with only a plain allowance never benches this way
fix: Define 'plain allowance' once: 'one number for all error kinds, as opposed to a different number per error kind'. Then say 'a lone copy with only a plain number is never benched by the counter; a per-error number for the matching error does bench it' (FAILURE-039).

lost: "Over half" and "all" are different tests; why? Also does a lone 429 go here?
fix: Put the two failure-rate tests side by side: not-lone copies: more than half of at least 5 requests failed; any copy: every one of at least 1000 requests failed. Say a lone 429 skips the 429 rule and goes to the 1000-all test (FAILURE-043), and, if the claims give a reason for the different tests, state it (FAILURE-043 gives none).

lost: retryable status: 408, 409, 429 or any status of 500 and above ... A status that is not retryable, such as 401 or 404, benches even a lone deployment
fix: Add one line explaining the logic ('statuses worth retrying are treated as maybe-temporary and wait for the rate tests; the others bench at once') and spell out what a non-lone 402 does: it falls through to the same last rule, so it benches at once (FAILURE-044). Give a table of 401/402/404/408/429/5xx x lone/not lone.

lost: per-minute counts: each server's own success and failure counts ... normally over a 60-second window from the first count
fix: Say 'a 60-second window that opens at the first count after the last one ran out; it does not slide, and it is not the clock minute'. Replace 'normally' with the one exception in plain words (when the server's small in-memory store is full and drops entries early, FAILURE-073), or drop the word.

lost: A pause shorter than one second stays on one server" and "Redis keeps whole seconds
fix: Say 'Redis cannot hold a time shorter than one second, so the shared copy of a half-second bench is refused and only the server that wrote it honors it'. Say once that the router runs as many servers sharing one store, and that 'this server' means the one handling the request.

lost: read interval: how often, at most, a server asks Redis about a bench it does not hold in its own memory
fix: Say what Redis is on first use: 'Redis, the shared in-memory database several router servers can use to share benches and counters'. Say that without it each server keeps its own benches.

lost: the error message with its first 50 characters kept and the rest starred
fix: Write 'the rest replaced with asterisks (*)'.

lost: Slack alert: ... sent only when Slack alerting is set up and the request did not come through the proxy
fix: Say what 'the proxy' is ('the separate gateway server that fronts the router; it reports its own failures') and say whether it is a different product from the router. Say who the customer is likely to run (router alone or behind the proxy), or drop the Slack row from this chapter since it is not part of the bench.

lost: health mark: a health check's verdict on a deployment; separate from a bench, it counts only when health-check routing is on
fix: Either drop the row, or add one sentence: 'health checks are a separate way a copy can be left out (a probe marks it unhealthy for up to 10 minutes); this chapter only covers benches after a failed call' (FAILURE-086).

lost: retry count: ... a retry skips a deployment that failed with a status that is not retryable ... A request that sets its own retry count to 0 turns the policy off; a router-wide 0 does not
fix: Start with 'the retry count is how many times the router resends a failed request to the same model name'. Then say what each 0 does: a request-level 0 means no retries and ignores the retry policy; a router-wide 0 is only the default, so a retry policy can still raise the count for a given error kind (RDISP-138).

lost: fallback depth: how many backup attempts deep a walk is; the maximum is checked only when a walk starts
fix: Put the 'Watch out' explanation first: 'the maximum number of fallbacks limits how deep backups can start backups of their own, not how many backups one list tries; with a maximum of 1 and three backups listed, all three are tried' (FAILURE-147). Rename the concept 'nesting depth'.

lost: nested walk" and "A backup call can nest
fix: Give the customer-facing reason: a backup model can itself have a backup list, so a request can hop A, then A's backup, then that one's backup; the depth maximum is what stops this, and the x-litellm-attempted-fallbacks header counts the depth, not the hops (FAILURE-213).

lost: an entry with extra settings counts apart from the bare model name" ... "an order level
fix: Show one backup-list entry with extra settings, for example a model name plus 'temperature 0', or a model name plus an order level (RDISP-104, the per-level entries order-based fallback builds), and say such an entry is a separate attempt from the bare name (FAILURE-109).

lost: An entry that is neither a model name nor a set of settings never counts as tried, so it can run again
fix: Say this is a misconfigured list entry (for example an empty value or a list inside the list) and that it re-calls the previous target; drop it from the plain layer if no customer would write one (FAILURE-184).

lost: Pinned provider resource
fix: Spell out in the figure 'Request refers to a file, batch or job at one provider?' and in the step say 'a file or batch lives at the provider that created it, so a backup model at another provider could not see it; the router keeps such requests on the original model name'.

lost: access and budget checks: two optional checks whoever builds the router can add
fix: Say who: 'the operator who sets up the router, or the proxy, which adds one that only lets a key call backup models it is allowed to use'. If the customer cannot add one, say so, and say the rows 'optional' means off unless the operator turns it on.

lost: fallback headers: x-litellm-attempted-retries ...
fix: Say once, in the first paragraph, that the product is called LiteLLM and the router is its component, and that header names start with 'x-litellm-' for that reason.

lost: error-list opt-in: a request setting that adds the fallback-errors header
fix: Name it: 'the caller adds include_fallback_errors to the request; the response then carries x-litellm-fallback-errors listing the failed backups' (FAILURE-150).

lost: The x-litellm-attempted-fallbacks header can undercount
fix: Say the consequence: 'a customer should not rely on this header to count how many backups were tried; when a backup reached the success through its own backup list, the header reports the outer number, so it can read 1 where two backups were tried' (FAILURE-216), and say what to use instead if anything.

lost: In the worked example, at 3s the error says "try again in 5" while the real wait is 2s
fix: Add to the 3s row of the timeline: 'real wait is 2 seconds, until dep-a returns at 5s; the 5 is the configured bench length, not the time left'.

lost: When no deployment of a model survives selection, cooldowns included" ... "in the usual case
fix: Write 'when selection finds no copy left for this model, whether benched or filtered out by other checks'. Name the unusual case or drop the phrase 'in the usual case'; the claims shown here say the error goes to backup handling and the original error is raised when no backup answers (RDISP-096, RDISP-115) and do not name an exception.

lost: Under default settings, a 429 or 5xx never benches a lone deployment unless all of at least 1000 requests in a minute failed
fix: Rewrite without 'never ... unless': 'A lone copy is benched by 429 or 5xx only if every one of at least 1000 requests in the last minute failed on this server.'

lost: connection-error text: the text "APIConnectionError" ... an error message containing it stops the bench at the status check
fix: Explain the reason, or say there is none: the claims list this as a suspected defect (FAILURE-209, FAILURE-202) because the check looks at the message text, not the error type, so a real outage that surfaces as a connection error does not bench the copy. Move it from a definition to a plain 'known gap' sentence.

lost: Prometheus metrics: ... each bench marks the deployment as out and adds one to its cooled-down count
fix: Say 'Prometheus is a monitoring system that collects numbers from the router; if the customer runs it, a bench shows as a copy marked out and a count of cool-downs per copy; if not, a bench leaves no number anywhere' (FAILURE-056).

lost: The title says "for seconds", but the cooldown time is ... else the error's retry-after header
fix: Say that a retry-after value of 0 or more from the provider sets the bench length and that the claims name no upper limit, so a long provider value benches the copy for that long (RDISP-191). Either change the title to 'for a short time' or add the caveat.

lost: 5xx" is used without saying it means any 5-hundred status
fix: Write 'a 5xx error (any status from 500 to 599)' at first use.

lost: Who would notice: only the 429 for callers and Prometheus numbers are named
fix: Add a short 'How you would see it' list: the bench writes no log and sends no alert; it shows as Prometheus numbers when Prometheus is set up, as the cooldown list inside the 429 'No deployments available' error text, and as the router's debug cooldown list (FAILURE-056, FAILURE-178, FAILURE-179).
